title: cursor/plugins — Cursor plugin specification and official plugins
content: Cursor plugins Official Cursor plugins for popular developer tools, frameworks, and SaaS products. Each plugin is a standalone directory at the repository root with its own .cursor-plugin/plugin.json manifest. The root .cursor-plugin/marketplace.json lists all plugins, and each plugin has its own manifest: plugins/ ├── .cursor-plugin/ │ └── marketplace.json # Marketplace manifest (lists all plugins) ├── plugin-name/ │ ├── .cursor-plugin/ │ │ └── plugin.json # Per-plugin manifest │ ├── skills/ # Agent skills (SKILL.md with frontmatter) │ ├── rules/ # Cursor rules (.mdc files) │ ├── mcp.json # MCP server definitions │ ├── README.md │ ├── CHANGELOG.md │ └── LICENSE └── ... report.summary: Cursor released an official multi-plugin marketplace repo with manifests, skills, rules, and MCP servers for many developer and SaaS tools.
report.background: Cursor has rapidly evolved from a code editor into a broader agentic development platform. This repository formalizes plugin distribution by introducing a standard manifest format (plugin.json and marketplace.json), along with directories for agent skills, rules, and MCP server definitions. By housing plugins for popular SaaS products, developer tools, and internal workflows, Cursor is standardizing how AI agents get context, execute actions, and integrate with external platforms. The move reflects the broader industry trend of making AI coding assistants extensible, auditable, and shareable through open-source packages. It also gives teams a structured way to publish custom functionality and maintain compatibility as Cursor's agent runtime evolves, ultimately laying groundwork for a more mature plugin ecosystem similar to VS Code's marketplace but tailored for agentic workflows.
key_points: The repo defines a clear multi-plugin repository structure: a root marketplace.json lists all plugins, while each plugin has its own .cursor-plugin/plugin.json manifest containing metadata, skills, rules, and MCP server definitions. This standardization makes sharing and discovery consistent.

Official plugins cover both developer-focused tools (GitHub, Playwright, CLI patterns, code review canvases) and productivity/integration SaaS products (Gmail, Salesforce, Zoom, HubSpot, Todoist, etc.), giving agents built-in capabilities to search, draft, and manage real-world workflows.

Several plugins emphasize structured agent behavior: continual-learning updates AGENTS.md from transcripts, pr-review-canvas renders diffs as prioritized canvases, and orchestrator fans work out to parallel cloud agents with verifiers. These go beyond simple tool wrappers to shape how agents reason and operate.

The repository is MIT-licensed and includes per-plugin README, CHANGELOG, and LICENSE files. This signals Cursor is inviting community contributions and enterprise adoption without restrictive licensing, encouraging practitioners to build and maintain their own plugins against stable conventions.

The listing includes experimental or humorous names (thermos, ralph-loop) alongside practical utilities. This indicates Cursor is testing various agent interaction patterns in public, hoping real-world usage will reveal which approaches improve reliability, security, and long-term memory for coding agents.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this repository formalizes plugin packaging for agentic coding environments, pushing toward a future where agents are as extensible as editors were in the past. Developers gain a clear reference for building their own plugins using skills, rules, and MCP servers, reducing guesswork around Cursor's internal conventions. Regular users benefit indirectly: integrations with services like Gmail, Salesforce, and GitHub mean agents can complete multi-step business tasks without leaving the editor. Teams can share internal workflows, CI checks, and verification logic more reliably. This also pressures competitors to define similar plugin ecosystems, accelerating interoperability and raising expectations for how coding assistants integrate with external tools and company knowledge.
report.tools: Readers should watch Cursor's TypeScript SDK (cursor-sdk) for building automations and the create-plugin scaffolder for bootstrapping new agents. The agent-compatibility and cli-for-agent plugins are useful references for designing reliable CLI-based integrations. Playwright plugin enables browser automation testing. Monitor MCP standards from the Model Context Protocol ecosystem since Cursor's mcp.json support ties directly into broader tool interoperability.
